text: So I mentioned to Jim that I wanted to go first tonight because I've been giving a lot of thought to what happened in the Capitol last week and it felt very poignant that we say the Pledge of Allegiance every Council meeting whether we're in person or not in light of and I think we often like so many kids in school we just think and go through the motions without really thinking about what it means. So I've just been giving a lot of thought and it just seems as we recite the Pledge of Allegiance tonight it's really important to reflect on what that sacred pledge really means in light of the horrific events of last week when the Capitol was overrun by a group of domestic terrorists who called themselves patriots. Every American should be appalled at the desecration of our flag and their feeble but deadly attempt to upend our democracy. I am particularly heartbroken for every service member and veteran who has proudly served defending our flag and particularly those that never came home and the American values and ideals that represents to have to bear witness to this assault on our democracy. This moment in history is one that will live far beyond us and it shows the deep divides that exist in this era of American democracy. It is my fervent hope that our country can begin to come together and heal in the weeks and the months ahead. My biggest wish above all else is that we can set that tone here in our own community and recommit ourselves to living up to the American ideals of freedom and tolerance. I pledge to do my part as the leader of this governing body. I know we have differences and we always will, but we cannot allow them to destroy our civility and erase our commonalities. Westfield has always prided itself on a very strong sense of community, perhaps never more so than the last year amidst this pandemic. And I know that sense of community will continue to see us through. We are and we will always be one nation under God. text: Bob. Right. Thanks, Jim. And good evening, everyone. So yeah, just a quick update. You know, this has been in the works and under development for several months now. The most recent development in the process of putting the program together was a little over a month ago when we submitted draft bidding documents to the Board of Public Utilities and Division of Rate Counsel for their review. This is essentially the request for proposals and then the form of contract. This is a step required in the process in the BPU's rules. So those documents were submitted about a month ago. We're now in a position to release the RFP and to actually start the competitive solicitation process. So we have an ad that was placed in the paper that will appear tomorrow. Tomorrow we'll be able to release the RFP and then start the solicitation process to attract BPU licensed suppliers to submit offers to the town for electric power supply for residents of the town. And the bid specifications that we're putting out specify that the renewable energy content of that power supply that we're asking for proposals on would be roughly a little less than twice the renewable energy content of what is provided by PSC&G. Just to put that in context, the current state requirement is that power supply provided by PSC&G and other suppliers must have at least 23.5 percent renewable energy. We are asking for a product that has 20 percent additional, so that would be a total of 43.5 percent renewable energy, so nearly half the renewable energy content. We'll be seeking proposals for that. The process is a two-stage process. The stage one is the qualification stage where we ask suppliers to submit their prior experience with this type of a program, a residential program, provide all their various legal documents that are required for the bidding process. Those are vetted, and then ultimately pricing proposals will be submitted on February 9th, and that date coincides with a town council meeting. So the way it works in the energy world, things move pretty quick. Energy markets are changing all the time, so we really need to make a contract award on the same evening that bids are submitted. So bids will be submitted on the deadline of noon on the 9th of February. We would then bring those results to the governing body for discussion and decision that evening whether or not to award a contract. We will be providing reports several days before bid day just to sort of give you an overview of the ratings of the qualifications of the suppliers that have been qualified, the benchmarking that we will use to evaluate the bids as compared to the PSE&G tariff. So when we have the bids come in, we will assess those bids as compared to where we see the PSE&G tariff falling, and obviously the goal is to obtain a contract that has power supply with significantly higher renewable energy content at a price that is lower than what PSE&G is charging for their power supply, which has less renewable content. So we're looking for and hoping for a win-win, but in the end, those bids are up to your final discretion as to whether or not you believe that the contract is beneficial enough to warrant an award. And if you deem so, we would move forward with a contract award and then start a process which would ensue over the next three months or so, which would include a mailing a notification, mailing to residents, and then a public information session of information being provided on the contract, a 30-day opt-out period, and then ultimately the ultimate goal would be for the contract to start in May, with May meter reads May of 2021. But again, that is all contingent upon the bids coming back at a price that you deem to be acceptable. If the contracts do not come in with a favorable enough price, then it is certainly within your discretion to not award a contract. And we'd sort of, you know, be status quo, you know, pending perhaps another venture in the future for a rebid. So that's, I guess, a good rundown of sort of where we are in the process and what the next steps might be. And obviously, I'm happy to answer any questions you have.

In addition to the renewable energy content, I think over the life of the contract, there were ebbs and flows of the PSE&G rate. Over the life of the contract, I think folks have saved a few dollars, certainly not a lot of money. You know, in the end, I think it was still a reasonably favorable story of power supply that had much higher renewable energy content and a price that came in on average, about equal to the PSE&G price. But I think there were perhaps some unrealistic expectations in terms of how the program was originally rolled out when the contract was first awarded. But I think folks did not necessarily see the level of savings that they were expecting. So I think that led to some of the, you know, some of the turmoil, if you will, with some residents sort of feeling that they did not see what they were expecting to see.
